nameStory: The brown-tail moth gets its straightforward name from the distinctive tuft of brown hairs at the tip of its abdomen, which looks like a fuzzy brown tail. This "tail" is especially prominent in females and serves as one of the moth's most recognizable features.
description: The brown-tail moth is a medium-sized white moth with a wingspan of about 1.5 inches. Adults are primarily bright white with a distinctive brown tuft of hairs at the end of their abdomen. The caterpillars are dark with orange spots and covered in irritating hairs that can cause skin rashes in humans. This European species has established populations along the Maine coast and is slowly expanding its range.

idTips.label: Brown tail tuft
idTips.description: Look for the characteristic cluster of brown, fuzzy hairs at the tip of the abdomen - it's like a small brown pompom that contrasts sharply with the white body

idTips.label: White wings and body
idTips.description: The wings and body are bright, clean white with a slightly silky sheen that catches light beautifully

idTips.label: Caterpillar appearance
idTips.description: Dark brown or black caterpillars with two bright orange spots on the back and covered in long, barbed hairs that feel irritating to touch

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Adults fly with a somewhat erratic, fluttering pattern and are strongly attracted to lights at night during summer

idTips.label: Web nests
idTips.description: Caterpillars create distinctive white silken webs in tree branches that look like large cotton balls or tissue paper clusters

habitat: Brown-tail moths are found primarily along the Maine coast and nearby islands, favoring areas with oak, apple, cherry, and other deciduous trees. They thrive in coastal environments, parks, residential areas with fruit trees, and forest edges. The species prefers warmer microclimates and is gradually expanding inland from its coastal strongholds.

seasonality.spring: Caterpillars emerge from overwintering webs and begin feeding actively on fresh leaves, creating new silk shelters in branches.
seasonality.summer: Adult moths emerge in July and August, flying at night and mating. This is the best time to see the distinctive white adults with brown tail tufts.
seasonality.fall: Young caterpillars construct their overwintering webs - conspicuous white silken nests that remain visible in bare trees after leaves drop.
seasonality.winter: Caterpillars remain dormant in their protective silk webs, which are easily spotted as white masses in leafless trees.

funFact: The brown-tail moth caterpillars have barbed hairs that can become airborne and cause skin rashes, respiratory problems, and eye irritation in humans even without direct contact - the hairs can blow on the wind for miles and remain irritating for up to three years after the caterpillar has molted!
confusionNotes: Adult brown-tail moths can be confused with other white moths, but the brown tail tuft is unique and diagnostic. The caterpillars might be mistaken for gypsy moth caterpillars, but brown-tails have orange spots while gypsy moths have blue and red spots in pairs.
contextualKnowledge: This is an invasive species from Europe that was accidentally introduced to Massachusetts in the 1890s and has become a significant pest. While populations crashed in most areas by the 1960s, they persist along the Maine coast and are considered both an ecological concern and a public health issue due to the irritating hairs.
compareHints: Since brown-tail moth is the only Euproctis species in New England, compare it to other white moths in the region. Unlike the fall webworm moth, brown-tail moths have the distinctive brown abdominal tuft and their caterpillars don't create large tent-like webs. White-marked tussock moths are much smaller and have different caterpillar coloration patterns.
